opus-5.5.text:
Going in, I think a lot of us had a fairly cautious view. We knew the models were getting very good at reasoning on paper: reading literature, proposing hypotheses, explaining mechanisms. The open question was whether any of that would hold up once it hit an actual wet lab, where biology is messy and most ideas don't work.

What changed my thinking was seeing the model take part in the experimental loop itself. Working with the Ginkgo team, we had GPT-5 propose experimental designs and protocol changes, then they ran them in the lab, and the results came back to the model to inform the next round. Some of what it suggested were things an experienced scientist might eventually try, but it got there faster and explored more of the space than a person usually has bandwidth for. A few suggestions were genuinely non-obvious, the kind of thing where the scientists said, "Huh, we wouldn't have thought to try that," and then it actually worked.

So for me it moved the question from "can AI help science in principle?" to "how do we best integrate it into the loop?" The model isn't replacing the scientist or the lab. Physical experiments are still the bottleneck and the ground truth. But when you pair a model that can generate and reason over lots of hypotheses with a lab that can test them quickly, the iteration speed goes up meaningfully, and in science iteration speed is a lot of what progress is.

It also made me more optimistic and more careful at the same time. Optimistic because the gains were real and measurable. Careful because once these systems meaningfully accelerate biology, you have to think seriously about how they're deployed, who has access to what, and the safeguards around that. Both of those became much more concrete for me after that work.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, going into it I was skeptical in the way I think a lot of people who've actually worked in a wet lab are skeptical. The failure mode I expected was that the model would be a very articulate literature reviewer. It would summarize what's known, suggest the obvious next experiment, and basically give you back the consensus of the field in nicer prose. That's useful, but it's not acceleration. Science doesn't get faster because someone writes a better abstract.

What changed my mind was watching the model operate inside an actual experimental loop rather than just talking about one. The setup with Ginkgo was that the model wasn't advising from the outside. It was proposing conditions, those conditions were getting run on their automated platform, the data came back, and the model had to look at results that were often messy or partially contradictory and decide what to do next. And the thing that surprised me was how it handled the second and third iteration, not the first. The first round is where you'd expect it to look smart, because it's basically pattern-matching to prior work. The later rounds are where you find out whether it can actually reason from evidence it hasn't seen before.

There was a stretch where it was optimizing a protocol, and the improvements it found weren't the ones a textbook would have pointed you toward. Some of them were things an experienced person in the lab might have tried eventually, but the model got there in a handful of cycles instead of weeks of someone's attention. And in a couple of cases it was willing to drop an assumption that was sitting in the standard method for historical reasons rather than good reasons. That's the part that felt qualitatively different to me. It wasn't being creative in some mystical sense. It was just not carrying the same inherited habits that a human scientist carries, and it could run many more hypotheses in parallel without getting attached to any of them.

I want to be careful not to overstate it, though. The model was wrong plenty of times. It proposed things that didn't work, and in a few instances it was confidently wrong in ways that a good postdoc would have caught before wasting a plate. The loop only worked because there was real-world feedback closing it every cycle and because the Ginkgo folks had the infrastructure to run experiments quickly and reliably. If you take the model out of that loop, you're back to the articulate literature reviewer problem.

So the update for me wasn't "AI can do science now." It was narrower and I think more important. It was that the bottleneck in a lot of experimental science is the cycle time between idea and data, and the model can meaningfully compress that when it's paired with automation and honest feedback. The questions it asked weren't always more profound than a human's, but it could ask a lot more of them, cheaply, and learn from the answers. That's a different kind of contribution than I was expecting, and it's one I now believe is real.

astra-6.text:
What changed for me was the distinction between having a model suggest an interesting idea and having that idea survive an actual experiment. To accelerate science, a model has to help us learn something about the world, not just produce a convincing explanation.

The GPT-5 work with Ginkgo brought that feedback loop into focus: propose something, test it, and use the result to decide what to try next. That’s where I see the potential—not just in generating more hypotheses, but in helping scientists choose more informative experiments.

I wouldn’t take one collaboration as proof that AI can accelerate every field. But it sharpened the question for me: can a model help us reach a useful result with less time and fewer experiments? That’s a concrete way to measure progress.

sol-6.1.text:
What changed for me was seeing the model’s ideas tested against a physical experiment. A model can propose something that sounds scientifically plausible, but the real question is: Does it work in the lab?

Working with Ginkgo gave us a way to close that loop—to have GPT-5 propose experiments, get results back, and use those results to decide what to try next. That’s a much stronger test than asking it to answer a science question where the answer is already known.

It made me more optimistic about AI accelerating science, but also more aware that the experimental infrastructure matters. You need reliable measurements and a way to feed the results back into the process. The exciting thing is the combination: a model that can help explore possibilities and a lab that can tell you which of those possibilities actually hold up.
